opus-5.5.text:
I think we're in a really unique moment. The biggest opportunity, from my perspective, is that 3D content creation has historically been extremely expensive and slow. If you want a high-quality 3D asset for a game, a film, or an AR/VR experience, you typically need a skilled artist spending days, sometimes weeks, on modeling, UV unwrapping, texturing, rigging. That bottleneck has limited how much 3D content the world can produce. With generative AI, we can compress that process from days to minutes, and that fundamentally changes who can create 3D content. Indie game developers, educators, 3D printing hobbyists, people who never learned Blender or Maya. That's the mission behind Meshy: making 3D creation accessible to everyone.

There's also a timing aspect. When I was working on Taichi and on physics simulation and graphics during my PhD, the tools were very much about helping experts be more productive. Now, with diffusion models and large-scale training, we can actually think about end-to-end generation. The foundation has matured enough that it's possible to build a real product, not just a research demo.

But the challenges are very real. First, 3D is much harder than 2D. With images, there are billions of training examples on the internet. High-quality 3D data is far scarcer, so you have to be very clever about data, about leveraging 2D priors, and about model architecture. Second, the bar for production use is high. A generated mesh has to have clean topology, good UVs, PBR textures, and work in existing pipelines like Unity, Unreal, or a 3D printer. Something that looks good in a render but breaks in a game engine isn't useful to professionals.

Third, the competitive landscape moves incredibly fast. Big tech companies and many well-funded startups are working on similar problems, and new open-source models come out almost every month. As a startup, you can't win just by having a slightly better model for three months. You have to build the full product experience, understand your users deeply, and iterate quickly. We focus a lot on listening to our community and shipping features that solve real workflow problems.

Finally, there's the question of how AI fits into creative work. Some artists are worried, and I understand that. My view is that, like many tools before it, AI will handle the repetitive, labor-intensive parts and let artists focus on creativity and taste. Our goal is to empower creators, not replace them. So overall, I'm very optimistic. It's hard, but that's what makes it exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says the AI foundation has matured enough to build a real product, but does not identify integrating vendors’ capabilities through APIs instead of building them in-house.

r002.rationale: It says the competitive landscape and new model releases move quickly, so a temporary model advantage is insufficient and the company must keep iterating and shipping features.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the first thing to say is that generative AI has completely reshaped what it even means to build a company like Meshy. When I was doing my PhD work on Taichi and physics simulation, 3D content creation was a world of specialists: artists spending days or weeks sculpting, retopologizing, UV unwrapping, texturing a single asset. The opportunity now is that the cost of producing a 3D asset is collapsing by orders of magnitude, in the same way image generation collapsed the cost of making a picture. That unlocks demand that never existed before, because so many people who had an idea for a game, a product, a virtual space, simply never had the budget or the skill to make the 3D content. We get to serve indie developers, hobbyists, educators, and also big studios who want to iterate faster.

The challenge is that 3D is fundamentally harder than images or text. The data is scarce; there are maybe millions of decent 3D assets in the world compared to billions of images. The output has to be geometrically correct, not just plausible-looking from one angle, and it has to fit into real production pipelines with clean topology, proper materials, rigging, and so on. A generated image is the final product. A generated mesh is usually the start of a workflow, so quality bar and interoperability matter enormously.

Then there's the competitive landscape. Everyone sees the same opportunity, large labs included, so the question is how you stay ahead. For us the answer has been focus: building a product that artists actually use every day, listening to that feedback loop, and investing deeply in the research side so we're not just wrapping someone else's model. The compute costs are real, the talent competition is real, and the pace means a six-month lead can evaporate. But honestly, I'd rather be building in this moment than any other. It's the first time I've felt that the tools I dreamed about as a graphics researcher are actually within reach.

r001.rationale: The response discusses investing in research and says Meshy is not just wrapping someone else’s model. It does not identify integrating vendors’ capabilities through APIs because the AI ecosystem is mature.

r002.rationale: It says the pace of AI can make a six-month lead evaporate, but does not connect that pace to a need for continual product updates to stay competitive.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunity is to make 3D creation accessible to many more people. You might have a clear picture in your head of a character or an object, but turning that into a 3D asset takes specialized skills and a lot of time. With generative AI, we can shorten that distance between having an idea and being able to create something with it. That’s an exciting opportunity for Meshy.

The challenge is that generating something that looks impressive is only part of the job. Can you control the result? Can you edit it? Can you actually use it in your project? Those questions matter a lot if you want people to use the product beyond their first experiment.

And the technology moves so quickly that we have to keep learning while still building a reliable product. I think the key is to stay close to users: understand where they get stuck, improve the things that save them time, and make the technology useful in their everyday work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making 3D creation accessible, but does not mention integrating vendors’ capabilities through APIs instead of building them in-house.

r002.rationale: It says AI technology moves quickly and Meshy must keep learning, but does not say continual product updates are needed to maintain a competitive position.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is that generative AI can make 3D creation accessible to many more people. Traditionally, turning an idea into a usable 3D asset takes specialized skills and a lot of time. With Meshy, we want to shorten that process so people can spend more time exploring ideas and creating things.

The challenge is that generating something that looks good is only part of the job. A 3D asset also needs to work in someone’s workflow. Depending on the use case, that can mean better geometry, useful textures, or more control over the result. There’s a big difference between a compelling demo and a tool people can depend on every day.

So I see the opportunity and the challenge as closely connected: make creation easier while giving users enough quality and control to do something meaningful with what they generate.

r001.rationale: It describes making 3D creation accessible and improving asset quality and control, but does not mention ecosystem maturity or integrating vendor capabilities through APIs.

r002.rationale: It notes the gap between demos and dependable tools, but does not identify rapid AI progress or the need for continual updates to stay competitive.
